newsitem.title: GERMANY: Austria's Klima says euro delay would be mistake.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Klima says euro delay would be mistake.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima said in an interview to be published Saturday that it would be a mistake from an economic point of view to delay the launch of the single European currency.

Klima, according to a text of an interview in the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Maastricht Treaty was flexible enough so that the decision to be made in early 1998 about the candidates for the euro's launch will be "wise" and not merely "mathematical".

"France is not thinking about a delay," Klima said. "France wants to include the subject of employment, which we support. And in Germany no one important is requesting a delay, not even (opposition leader Oskar) Lafontaine.
"A delay would be not only economically nonsense, but it would also endanger the whole project," Klima said.
He said he was opposed to relaxing the Maastricht Treaty criteria for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), but said there was room for a somewhat less stringent interpretation of the criteria.
"The flexibility of the treaty makes it possible that the decision in 1998 does not have to be a mathematical one, but rather can be a wise one," Klima said.

"But it is not true that the state debt may not exceed 60 percent of gross domestic product. The treaty says that what is to be considered is whether the debt level is moving in the right direction at the right speed."

Klima said that even though German Finance Minister Theo Waigel is right to say the budget deficit should not exceed three percent, his experience as chief financial officer of Austria's largest oil company OMV taught him there was some room for flexibility in every budget and target.
Asked if he was suggesting "creative accounting" Klima said:
"A finance minister can do such a thing," said Klima, who was also Austria's finance minister before he became chancellor.

"The European project can not be allowed to fail because of the accounting practices. That fails to recognise the political dimension of the project. I believe the euro is a further step against decline, renationalisation and chauvinism."
